label: Work and Burnout
framing: Burnout is not always a sign you are doing too little. Often it is the sign of a body and soul kept under load that God never asked you to carry, with no rhythm to set it down. Scripture treats your labor as good and your limits as built in, not as flaws to be overcome.
cultural: Most people in the biblical world worked the land or a trade from dawn to dark, and the threat was never idleness but a master, a debt, or a harvest that demanded everything. Into that grind God wrote a weekly stop into the law itself, and called it freedom, since only a slave is denied rest. Even Israel's fields were given a year off.
historical: The monastic rule of Benedict in the sixth century ordered the day into work, prayer, and rest so that no one part swallowed the others, and the church carried that balance for a thousand years. The Reformers later raised ordinary work to a calling, though their heirs sometimes turned that gift into the engine of a relentless striving the Sabbath was meant to break.
application: Treat your limits as a message, not an enemy, and ask what the exhaustion is trying to tell you. Build a real stop into your week and defend it before the work eats it. Refuse the lie that your worth rises and falls with your output. And if the burnout has hollowed out your sleep, your joy, and your love for the people closest to you, get help, because that is not weakness but stewardship of the one body you were given.

verses.text: For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident.
verses.where: For six days Israel is to work, and on the seventh to stop, so that the ox and the donkey may rest and the servant's son and the foreigner may be refreshed. The site's note sets the weekly Sabbath beside the sabbatical year and the laws for honest courts. The rest is given for those with the least power to take it.

verses.text: Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work—neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant, nor your ox or donkey or any of your livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates, so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do. Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. That is why the LORD your God has commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.
verses.where: Moses repeats the Sabbath command, so that servants may rest as their masters do, and gives the reason: remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD brought you out. The site's note says he insists the covenant was made with the generation standing in front of him. Rest is how a freed people remembers that it is no longer enslaved.

verses.text: But Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good. Surely you and these people with you will wear yourselves out, because the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone.
verses.where: Watching Moses judge the people from morning to evening, his father-in-law Jethro tells him that what he is doing is not good: he and the people will wear themselves out, and he cannot handle it alone. The site's note says Jethro has Moses appoint capable, God-fearing men to share the load, and Moses does. The faithful answer to an impossible load was to share it.

verses.text: Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.
verses.where: Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind. The site's note says the Teacher sees that much labor springs from envy, and meets a man who toils alone with no heir and no rest. That man asks himself the question many overworked people never stop to ask: for whom am I doing this?

verses.text: For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun? Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile. Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.
verses.where: The Teacher asks what a person gets for all his toil, when his days are full of grief and even at night his mind does not rest, and then says nothing is better than to eat and drink and enjoy one's work, which is from the hand of God. The site's note says this is not resigned pleasure-seeking, because apart from God no one can enjoy anything. The same work that wears a person down can be received as a gift.

verses.text: Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself. When you glance at wealth, it disappears, for it makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky.
verses.where: Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself, for wealth sprouts wings and flies off like an eagle. The site's note sets it among the words of the wise on the fleeting nature of wealth. Proverbs counts knowing when to stop as wisdom.

verses.text: Meanwhile, the people of Judah said: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.”
verses.where: Rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, the people of Judah say the strength of the laborers is failing and there is so much rubble they will never finish. The site's note says Nehemiah prays, posts guards and rallies the discouraged people, and the work goes on. Exhausted workers were answered with prayer and with practical change together.

verses.text: Then Jesus declared, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”
verses.where: Defending his hungry disciples, Jesus says the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. The site's note says the Sabbath is a gift created for human good, and the plain note asks whether our habits give rest or are a load carried to prove ourselves. Rest was made to serve people, not to be one more thing to perform.

verses.text: Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.
verses.where: James warns rich landowners that the wages they withheld from the workers who mowed their fields cry out against them, and that the harvesters' cries have reached the Lord. The site's plain note says that if you have been cheated or crushed by the powerful, God has heard the cries, and the last word is his. Some burnout comes from injustice, and Scripture names it as injustice.

verses.text: Man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening.
verses.where: In a hymn to the Creator who sets the moon to mark the seasons and the sun to know its setting, man goes out to his work and to his labor until evening. The site's note says all living things depend on God for food and breath. In God's ordering of the day, work has an evening.

misread.taken: If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat is quoted at people who are burned out, ill or out of work, as if needing rest or being unable to keep going were laziness.
misread.says: The site's plain note says the word is unwilling, not unable: Paul is speaking of particular people in that church who could work, refused, and lived off others. It says the verse is never a word against the poor, the sick, the disabled, people who cannot find work, people caring for others, or people who receive help, and that using it that way goes against the letter it comes from.
misread.text: For even while we were with you, we gave you this command: “If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.”

whole: If burnout has come with despair, with thoughts of hurting yourself, or with weeks of lost sleep and appetite, tell someone you trust today, a doctor, a pastor or a friend, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Burnout at work often looks like dreading Monday from Saturday afternoon, answering messages at midnight, growing cynical about work you once loved, being too tired on the weekend to enjoy it. Some people are in jobs that ask too much; some work for employers who do not pay fairly or treat people well; some drive themselves harder than any boss would. Many cannot imagine stopping, because the bills, the team or their own sense of worth seem to depend on it.

Scripture treats work as good and limits as built in. God gave Israel a seventh day on which no one worked, not the servant, not the foreigner, not even the ox, and Deuteronomy ties that rest to memory: remember that you were a slave in Egypt. A life with no rest is lived as if we were still slaves. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes saw a man who toiled alone with no end to his labor and never asked for whom he was working, and he saw that much labor springs from envy of a neighbor. He also knew the mind that does not rest even at night. Some of what drives burnout is outside us, unfair pay and impossible demands, and James says the cries of cheated workers reach the Lord. Some is inside us: wanting more, fearing to be seen as less, believing our worth is what we produce. Most of us carry some of each.

So the Bible's wisdom is to keep the limits God gave. Six days of work and a day of rest is a command, given so that the tired would be refreshed, and Jesus said the Sabbath was made for man. Jethro told Moses that the way he was working was not good and would wear him out, and the answer was to share the load. Proverbs says not to wear yourself out to get rich, and to be wise enough to stop. Ecclesiastes says one handful with quiet is better than two with toil and chasing the wind, and that the ability to enjoy work is itself from the hand of God. When the builders' strength failed in Nehemiah's day, he prayed, set guards and rallied the people; burnout usually needs both prayer and a practical change. That may mean a hard conversation with a manager, a different job, or a doctor's help, and the site's plain note on 2 Corinthians 4 says seeking help is not a failure of faith.

The hope Scripture gives is that your work is not your worth. The site's plain note on 2 Thessalonians 3 says the saying about not eating is never a word against the sick or against those who cannot work. Psalm 104 says people go out to their work and labor until evening; work has an evening, and so do you. The God who rested on the seventh day made the Sabbath for us, and the cries of the overworked reach his ears.
deep.sit: What would it take to keep one full day this week on which your work does not get the last word?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says verse 7 gives words for a restless mind: when your heart is still racing after a hard time, say to yourself what this man said, return to your rest, O my soul.
prayer.text: The LORD is gracious and righteous; our God is full of compassion. The LORD preserves the simplehearted; I was helpless, and He saved me. Return to your rest, O my soul, for the LORD has been good to you. For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling. I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
Seeking help is not a failure of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
